easy.question: Who heard the news about the capture of Ai?
answers: Adoni‑zedek, king of Jerusalem
Joshua son of Nun
The king of Ai
easy.explanation: The verse opens 'Now it came to pass, when Adonizedec king of Jerusalem had heard…' — he is the one who heard.

easy.question: Which city had Joshua taken according to the verse?
answers: Gibeon
Ai
Jericho
easy.explanation: The verse says Joshua had taken Ai — Ai is the city captured.

easy.question: What was done to Ai as had been done to Jericho?
answers: It was rebuilt
It was spared
It was devoted/destroyed (devoted to destruction)
easy.explanation: The verse says he did to Ai 'as he had done to Jericho' — i.e., it was devoted (destroyed) as Jericho had been.

medium.question: Why was Adoni‑zedek greatly afraid?
answers: Because Joshua had conquered the whole land
Because Gibeon was a great city, one of the royal cities, larger than Ai and all its men were mighty
Because he received a threatening letter
medium.explanation: The verse explains they feared because Gibeon was a great royal city, greater than Ai, and all its men were strong.

medium.question: How does the text describe Gibeon in relation to Ai?
answers: Gibeon was smaller than Ai
Ai was greater than Gibeon
Gibeon was greater than Ai
medium.explanation: The verse explicitly says Gibeon was greater than Ai.

medium.question: What does the phrase 'one of the royal cities' imply about Gibeon?
answers: That it was a small unimportant town
That it was a capital of a foreign empire
That it was one of the important/regional cities of the area
medium.explanation: 'One of the royal cities' indicates a high standing among the region’s cities — Gibeon was considered important.

challenge.question: What practical threat did Adoni‑zedek face when the verse says the inhabitants of Gibeon were 'mighty'?
answers: A threat only to water sources
An increase in Israel’s military strength because an important city with warriors sided with them
Only an economic loss
challenge.explanation: The verse notes 'all the men thereof were mighty' — joining with Israel strengthened their military capability.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'were among them' (the people of Gibeon being 'among them') suggest about Gibeon's relation to Israel?
answers: That Gibeon became part of the people and lived among them (joined Israel)
That Gibeon was destroyed and erased
That Gibeon remained hostile within Israel
challenge.explanation: 'Were among them' implies integration or being within Israel — the Gibeonites were with Israel.

challenge.question: How would you summarize Adoni‑zedek’s reaction to the Gibeonites making peace with Israel?
answers: He ignored it
He was alarmed and sought allies to attack Gibeon
He immediately made peace as well
challenge.explanation: He feared the alliance and called other kings to help attack Gibeon.

questions.question: What practical threat did Adoni‑zedek faced when the verse says the inhabitants of Gibeon were 'mighty'?
answers: A threat only to water sources
An increase in Israel’s military strength because an important city with warriors sided with them
Only an economic loss
questions.explanation: The verse notes 'all the men thereof were mighty' — joining with Israel strengthened their military capability.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'were among them' (the people of Gibeon being 'among them') suggest about Gibeon's relation to Israel?
answers: That Gibeon became part of the people and lived among them (joined Israel)
That Gibeon was destroyed and erased
That Gibeon remained hostile within Israel
questions.explanation: 'Were among them' implies integration or being within Israel — the Gibeonites were with Israel.

questions.question: How would you summarize Adoni‑zedek’s reaction to the Gibeonites making peace with Israel?
answers: He ignored it
He was alarmed and sought allies to attack Gibeon
He immediately made peace as well
questions.explanation: He feared the alliance and called other kings to help attack Gibeon.

easy.question: Who sent to the other kings asking for help against Gibeon?
answers: Adoni‑zedek king of Jerusalem
Joshua
The men of Gibeon
easy.explanation: Verse 3 says Adoni‑zedek sent to the other kings.

easy.question: What did Adoni‑zedek ask the kings to do?
answers: Make a peace treaty with Gibeon
Come up and help him to smite Gibeon
Send envoys to negotiate
easy.explanation: He asked them to come up and help him smite Gibeon.

easy.question: How many kings gathered to fight against Gibeon?
answers: Three
Eight
Five
easy.explanation: Verse 5 lists the five kings of the Amorites who gathered.

medium.question: What does the text mean when it says Gibeon 'had made peace with Joshua' in this context?
answers: That Gibeon had made a treaty or alliance with Joshua/Israel
That Gibeon betrayed Joshua
That Gibeon attacked Joshua
medium.explanation: In context, 'made peace' means they made a treaty or covenant with Joshua and Israel, prompting the attack.

medium.question: Where did the kings encamp and make war according to the verse?
answers: On Gibeon
At Jericho
At Shechem
medium.explanation: The verse says they encamped before Gibeon and made war against it.

medium.question: What did the men of Gibeon send to Joshua at Gilgal?
answers: A request to delay action
A plea to come quickly and save/help them
An offer to pay tribute
medium.explanation: They asked Joshua to come quickly, save them, and help them because the Amorite kings had gathered against them.

challenge.question: Why is it likely the Amorite kings attacked Gibeon according to the narrative?
answers: To expand their rule only
Because Gibeon had made a treaty with Joshua and Israel
Because Gibeon had offered them tribute
challenge.explanation: The text states Gibeon 'had made peace with Joshua' — the kings attacked because Gibeon chose Israel's side.

challenge.question: To which place did Gibeon's messengers go to reach Joshua?
answers: To the camp at Mount Gerizim
To the king's house in Jerusalem
To Joshua at the camp in Gilgal
challenge.explanation: Verse 6 explicitly says they sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'all the kings of the Amorites that dwell in the mountains' indicate?
answers: They were coastal kings
They were kings living in the hill country (mountain dwellers)
They were priests of Gibeon
challenge.explanation: It indicates they were kings of the highland/hill country — mountain-dwelling Amorite kings.

questions.question: Why is it likely the Amorite kings attacked Gibeon according to the narrative?
answers: To expand their rule only
Because Gibeon had made a treaty with Joshua and Israel
Because Gibeon had offered them tribute
questions.explanation: The text states Gibeon 'had made peace with Joshua' — the kings attacked because Gibeon chose Israel's side.

questions.question: To which place did Gibeon's messengers go to reach Joshua?
answers: To the camp at Mount Gerizim
To the king's house in Jerusalem
To Joshua at the camp in Gilgal
questions.explanation: Verse 6 explicitly says they sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'all the kings of the Amorites that dwell in the mountains' indicate?
answers: They were coastal kings
They were kings living in the hill country (mountain dwellers)
They were priests of Gibeon
questions.explanation: It indicates they were kings of the highland/hill country — mountain-dwelling Amorite kings.

paragraphs.title: Joshua sets out and a divine response

easy.question: Who went up from Gilgal with all the warriors?
answers: Joshua and all the men of war with him
Only Joshua
The Lord alone
easy.explanation: Verse 7 states Joshua went up from Gilgal with all the people of war and the mighty men of valour.

easy.question: What did the LORD say to Joshua to reassure him?
answers: 'Do not fear them'
'Stay in Gilgal'
'Return home'
easy.explanation: The LORD told Joshua 'Fear them not: for I have delivered them into thine hand'.

easy.question: When did Joshua come upon the Amorites?
answers: In the evening
At break of dawn
Suddenly all night
easy.explanation: Verse 9 says Joshua came upon them suddenly and went up from Gilgal all night.

medium.question: According to the passage, what caused more deaths than Israel's sword?
answers: Great hailstones (stones from heaven)
Internal clashes among the Amorites
A collapse of their encampments
medium.explanation: Verse 11 states that more died from hailstones cast from heaven than those Israel killed with the sword.

medium.question: How does the text describe the effect on the Amorites before Israel?
answers: They were put into confusion/panic (routed)
They celebrated victory
They successfully regrouped
medium.explanation: The LORD 'discomfited' them before Israel — the description and subsequent pursuit indicate confusion and rout.

medium.question: Why, according to verse 8, would no man of them stand before Joshua?
answers: Because they were weak and insignificant
Because the LORD had delivered them into Joshua's hand
Because the day was stormy
medium.explanation: Verse 8 explains 'for I have delivered them into thine hand' — the LORD granted Joshua victory, so they would not stand against him.

challenge.question: Which sequence of events matches the text?
answers: Joshua ascended from Gilgal → the LORD said 'Fear not' → Joshua came suddenly at night → the LORD struck them at Gibeon → the LORD cast hailstones from heaven
The LORD said 'Fear not' → Joshua ascended from Gilgal → the LORD cast hailstones → Joshua came at night → the LORD struck them at Gibeon
Joshua came at night → the LORD struck them at Gibeon → the LORD said 'Fear not' → Joshua ascended from Gilgal
challenge.explanation: The narrative: Joshua ascended (v7), the LORD spoke to him (v8), Joshua came suddenly at night (v9), the LORD discomfited them at Gibeon (v10), and then cast down hailstones (v11).

challenge.question: To which two places does the pursuit reach according to verse 10?
answers: Gibeon and upper Beth‑horon
Azekah and Makkedah
Gilgal and Beth‑horon
challenge.explanation: Verse 10 lists Azekah and Makkedah as the places where they were smitten in the pursuit.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'in the going down to Beth‑horon' imply about the direction of the flight?
answers: They climbed toward Beth‑horon up into the hills
They were descending toward Beth‑horon in flight (going down)
Beth‑horon was the Israelites' supply base
challenge.explanation: 'In the going down' indicates they were descending toward Beth‑horon while fleeing; the text describes their flight route.

questions.question: Which sequence of events matches the text?
answers: Joshua ascended from Gilgal → the LORD said 'Fear not' → Joshua came suddenly at night → the LORD struck them at Gibeon → the LORD cast hailstones from heaven
The LORD said 'Fear not' → Joshua ascended from Gilgal → the LORD cast hailstones → Joshua came at night → the LORD struck them at Gibeon
Joshua came at night → the LORD struck them at Gibeon → the LORD said 'Fear not' → Joshua ascended from Gilgal
questions.explanation: The narrative: Joshua ascended (v7), the LORD spoke to him (v8), Joshua came suddenly at night (v9), the LORD discomfited them at Gibeon (v10), and then cast down hailstones (v11).

questions.question: To which two places does the pursuit reach according to verse 10?
answers: Gibeon and upper Beth‑horon
Azekah and Makkedah
Gilgal and Beth‑horon
questions.explanation: Verse 10 lists Azekah and Makkedah as the places where they were smitten in the pursuit.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'in the going down to Beth‑horon' imply about the direction of the flight?
answers: They climbed toward Beth‑horon up into the hills
They were descending toward Beth‑horon in flight (going down)
Beth‑horon was the Israelites' supply base
questions.explanation: 'In the going down' indicates they were descending toward Beth‑horon while fleeing; the text describes their flight route.

paragraphs.title: The sun and moon stand still

easy.question: To whom did Joshua speak at the start of this section (verse 12)?
answers: The LORD
The Amorite kings
All Israel
easy.explanation: The verse begins 'Then spake Joshua to the LORD' — he addressed the LORD.

easy.question: Where is the moon mentioned as standing while the sun 'stood still'?
answers: At Gibeon
At Gilgal
In the valley of Ajalon (Ajalon/valley of Ajalon)
easy.explanation: The verse says 'and the moon in the valley of Ajalon' — the moon is described as standing there.

easy.question: Where did Joshua and all Israel return at the end of this passage (verse 15)?
answers: To Gibeon
To the camp at Gilgal
To Jerusalem
easy.explanation: Verse 15 ends with 'and Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.'

medium.question: Why were the sun and moon stopped according to the verses?
answers: To punish the enemies only
So that Israel could complete avenging themselves on their enemies (so the people could finish the battle)
So a written record would be created
medium.explanation: The text explains the sun stood still 'that the people might be stayed still upon their enemies' — the aim was to allow Israel to finish the battle.

medium.question: What does the phrase 'the sun stood still' mean in this context?
answers: That the sun stopped moving and the day was prolonged
That the sun became red
That the sun set early
medium.explanation: Here 'the sun stood still' is described as the sun ceasing to move — the day was prolonged until Israel avenged themselves.

medium.question: What does 'Is not this written in the book of Jasher?' suggest about the event?
answers: That the event was invented later
That an older source (the book of Jasher) also recorded the event
That 'Jasher' is a place name
medium.explanation: The mention suggests the event was also recorded in another ancient source called the book of Jasher, indicating an additional record of the tradition.

challenge.question: What can be inferred from the phrase 'the sun stood still in the midst of heaven' about the sun's position that day?
answers: That the sun was high in the sky (near its height) when it stopped
That the sun had already set below the horizon
That clouds hid the sun
challenge.explanation: 'In the midst of heaven' implies the sun was high in the sky when it stood still, not setting.

challenge.question: What theological claim is made by the statement 'for the LORD fought for Israel'?
answers: That the battle was solely a human achievement
That the LORD intervened on Israel's behalf and gave them victory
That Joshua alone was responsible for the victory
challenge.explanation: The verse attributes the victory to divine intervention — the LORD fought for Israel.

challenge.question: What does the reference to an external written source ('book of Jasher') imply about the tradition of this event?
answers: That the account was purely invented late with no parallel record
That the event was also written in another earlier/independent record
That 'book of Jasher' is a personal name of someone present
challenge.explanation: The citation implies there was another written tradition (the book of Jasher) that also recorded the event, suggesting it was not only oral.

questions.question: What can be inferred from the phrase 'the sun stood still in the midst of heaven' about the sun's position that day?
answers: That the sun was high in the sky (near its height) when it stopped
That the sun had already set below the horizon
That clouds hid the sun
questions.explanation: 'In the midst of heaven' implies the sun was high in the sky when it stood still, not setting.

questions.question: What theological claim is made by the statement 'for the LORD fought for Israel'?
answers: That the battle was solely a human achievement
That the LORD intervened on Israel's behalf and gave them victory
That Joshua alone was responsible for the victory
questions.explanation: The verse attributes the victory to divine intervention — the LORD fought for Israel.

questions.question: What does the reference to an external written source ('book of Jasher') imply about the tradition of this event?
answers: That the account was purely invented late with no parallel record
That the event was also written in another earlier/independent record
That 'book of Jasher' is a personal name of someone present
questions.explanation: The citation implies there was another written tradition (the book of Jasher) that also recorded the event, suggesting it was not only oral.

paragraphs.title: The kings flee and further fighting

easy.question: Where did the five kings flee and hide?
answers: In a cave at Makkedah
In the hills of Hebron
To the sea coast
easy.explanation: Verse 16 states the five kings fled and hid in a cave at Makkedah.

easy.question: What was reported to Joshua about the kings (verse 17)?
answers: They had surrendered with honors
They were found hiding in a cave at Makkedah
They had escaped to another land
easy.explanation: The report was that the five kings were found hiding in a cave at Makkedah.

easy.question: What did Joshua order to be done at the mouth of the cave?
answers: Leave it open and guard it lightly
Roll great stones to the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them
Fill the cave with water
easy.explanation: Joshua told them to roll great stones to the mouth of the cave and appoint guards to watch it.

medium.question: What did Joshua instruct his men regarding pursuit of the enemy?
answers: Stay back and negotiate a settlement
Pursue them and strike the rear so they do not reach their cities
Only take prisoners and release them later
medium.explanation: Joshua ordered them to pursue their enemies, smite the hindermost, and not let them enter their cities.

medium.question: Why were they told 'do not allow them to go back into their cities'?
answers: Because the LORD had delivered them into Israel's hand and they must not be allowed to regroup
To allow the enemy to regroup safely
To collect taxes from those cities later
medium.explanation: The reason given is that the LORD had delivered them into Israel's hand; letting them return to their cities would enable them to recover.

medium.question: What happened to the survivors after the great slaughter?
answers: They were executed immediately on the spot
They fled into fortified cities (the survivors entered fenced cities)
They were granted asylum by neighboring nations
medium.explanation: The text says the remnant entered into fenced cities — survivors fled to fortified towns.

challenge.question: What practical reason explains Joshua's order to block the cave with stones and leave guards?
answers: To prevent the kings from escaping and later rallying again
To make an architectural monument of the capture
To use the stones for building city walls later
challenge.explanation: Blocking the cave and posting guards was meant to ensure the kings could not escape and rejoin the fight later.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'a very great slaughter, until they were consumed' imply about the scope of the attack?
answers: The attack was only partial
The attack was carried out to complete destruction — thorough annihilation
The attack was postponed due to weather
challenge.explanation: The expression indicates the slaughter continued until it fulfilled its purpose — complete destruction of the force.

challenge.question: What was the state of the people after these events according to verse 21?
answers: They retreated in disorder and lost control
All the people returned to the camp at Makkedah in peace, none complained against Israel
They split into factions and fought among themselves
challenge.explanation: Verse 21 says all returned to the camp at Makkedah in peace and none objected against Israel.

questions.question: What practical reason explains Joshua's order to block the cave with stones and leave guards?
answers: To prevent the kings from escaping and later rallying again
To make an architectural monument of the capture
To use the stones for building city walls later
questions.explanation: Blocking the cave and posting guards was meant to ensure the kings could not escape and rejoin the fight later.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'a very great slaughter, until they were consumed' imply about the scope of the attack?
answers: The attack was only partial
The attack was carried out to complete destruction — thorough annihilation
The attack was postponed due to weather
questions.explanation: The expression indicates the slaughter continued until it fulfilled its purpose — complete destruction of the force.

questions.question: What was the state of the people after these events according to verse 21?
answers: They retreated in disorder and lost control
All the people returned to the camp at Makkedah in peace, none complained against Israel
They split into factions and fought among themselves
questions.explanation: Verse 21 says all returned to the camp at Makkedah in peace and none objected against Israel.

easy.question: Who commanded that the mouth of the cave be opened and the five kings brought out?
answers: Joshua
The captains of the army
The priests
easy.explanation: The passage begins 'Then said Joshua' — Joshua ordered the cave opened and the kings brought out.

easy.question: How did the men of war set their feet on the kings?
answers: They put their hands on the kings' heads
They set their feet upon the necks of the kings
They sat beside them and guarded them
easy.explanation: The text says they put their feet on the necks of the kings.

easy.question: What was done to the kings after Joshua pronounced judgment?
answers: They were released to return to their cities
They were tried in the city court
They were killed and hanged on five trees until evening
easy.explanation: Joshua had them slain and hanged on trees until evening.

medium.question: Which five kings were brought out of the cave?
answers: The king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon
The king of Shechem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jerusalem, the king of the north, the king of Eglon
The king of Jerusalem, the king of Bethlehem, the king of Lachish, the king of Gaza, the king of Eglon
medium.explanation: The verse lists those five specific kings: Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon.

medium.question: What happened to the bodies at sunset according to the narrative?
answers: They were left hanging indefinitely
They were taken down, cast into the cave where they had hidden, and great stones were laid at the cave's mouth
They were given a royal burial by Israel
medium.explanation: At sunset Joshua commanded they be taken down, cast into the cave, and great stones rolled to the mouth of the cave.

medium.question: Why did Joshua say 'Be not afraid, nor dismayed; be strong and of good courage' before executing the kings?
answers: To prepare for a new campaign
To encourage his soldiers and remind them the LORD would act against their enemies
To calm the captured kings
medium.explanation: Joshua's words were meant to encourage his troops, assuring them the LORD would act for Israel against their enemies.

challenge.question: What did they do with the bodies 'until this very day' according to the verse?
answers: They placed the stones and the blocked cave as a lasting memorial that remained to that day
They immediately removed the stones and buried the bodies elsewhere
They burned the cave as a warning to others
challenge.explanation: The text says the stones remained at the cave's mouth 'until this very day', indicating a lasting memorial or marker.

challenge.question: What does the continued presence of those stones 'until this day' suggest about the event's remembrance?
answers: It was forgotten quickly
It was kept as a visible memorial and remembered over time
It was a secret never spoken of again
challenge.explanation: Keeping the stones suggests the event was preserved in the landscape as a memorial and reminder.

challenge.question: What can be inferred from the list of cities named (Lachish, Hebron, Jerusalem, etc.) about the area of conflict?
answers: That the battles were in far northern territories like Mount Hermon
That the fighting took place in the hill country of Judah and the Shephelah (area around Hebron and Lachish)
That the campaign was in the southernmost Negev desert
challenge.explanation: The named cities indicate the conflict was in the region of Judah and its environs — the hill country and Shephelah.

questions.question: What did they do with the bodies 'until this very day' according to the verse?
answers: They placed the stones and the blocked cave as a lasting memorial that remained to that day
They immediately removed the stones and buried the bodies elsewhere
They burned the cave as a warning to others
questions.explanation: The text says the stones remained at the cave's mouth 'until this very day', indicating a lasting memorial or marker.

questions.question: What does the continued presence of those stones 'until this day' suggest about the event's remembrance?
answers: It was forgotten quickly
It was kept as a visible memorial and remembered over time
It was a secret never spoken of again
questions.explanation: Keeping the stones suggests the event was preserved in the landscape as a memorial and reminder.

questions.question: What can be inferred from the list of cities named (Lachish, Hebron, Jerusalem, etc.) about the area of conflict?
answers: That the battles were in far northern territories like Mount Hermon
That the fighting took place in the hill country of Judah and the Shephelah (area around Hebron and Lachish)
That the campaign was in the southernmost Negev desert
questions.explanation: The named cities indicate the conflict was in the region of Judah and its environs — the hill country and Shephelah.

easy.question: Who took Makkedah on that day?
answers: Joshua
The tribe of Judah
Its own king
easy.explanation: Verse 28 states that Joshua took Makkedah that day.

easy.question: Where did Joshua and all Israel go after Makkedah?
answers: Yavneh
Jericho
Libnah
easy.explanation: Verse 29 says Joshua and all Israel passed from Makkedah to Libnah.

easy.question: What happened to Libnah according to the verses?
answers: It was left largely intact
It was given into Israel's hand and none were left — utterly destroyed
It became a vassal city
easy.explanation: The verse notes the LORD gave Libnah into Israel's hand and none were left — it was utterly destroyed.

medium.question: What fate befell the king and inhabitants of Makkedah?
answers: The king was spared and the people enslaved
They were devoted to destruction; none were left
They were integrated peacefully into Israel
medium.explanation: The verse says Joshua utterly destroyed the king and all the souls in the city and left none remaining — they were devoted to destruction.

medium.question: What happened to Libnah according to the verse 'the LORD also gave it' — who delivered the city into Israel's hand?
answers: The king of Makkedah
The LORD
Joshua alone by his own power
medium.explanation: The text explicitly says the LORD gave the city into Israel's hand.

medium.question: What does the repetition 'left none remaining' in these cases emphasize?
answers: That mercy was consistently shown to some kings
That the devotion/destruction (the ban) and total destruction was absolute and repeated policy
That people were typically taken as captives for labor
medium.explanation: The repeated phrase underscores that the cities were devoted to destruction (the ban) and the policy was total annihilation in these instances.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'did to the king of Makkedah as he did to the king of Jericho' indicate?
answers: That Joshua treated their kings differently
That the king of Makkedah received the same fate as the king of Jericho — destruction under the ban
That the king of Jericho helped Makkedah
challenge.explanation: The comparison indicates the same treatment: devotion and destruction like Jericho's king.

challenge.question: What does the short phrasing 'and he passed... and fought' suggest about the conduct of the campaign?
answers: That the fighting followed long negotiations
That Joshua moved quickly from city to city in a swift campaign of consecutive battles
That there were long pauses between attacks
challenge.explanation: The terse wording implies rapid movement and consecutive engagements — a swift campaign.

challenge.question: What does 'devoted to destruction' (the ban) reflect about the policy in these conquests?
answers: That cities were usually annexed and their inhabitants integrated
That certain cities were completely destroyed as a religious/military policy
That they only took valuables and left people alive
challenge.explanation: The ban (herem) denotes total destruction or dedication to destruction, not integration or mere plunder.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'did to the king of Makkedah as he did to the king of Jericho' indicate?
answers: That Joshua treated their kings differently
That the king of Makkedah received the same fate as the king of Jericho — destruction under the ban
That the king of Jericho helped Makkedah
questions.explanation: The comparison indicates the same treatment: devotion and destruction like Jericho's king.

questions.question: What does the short phrasing 'and he passed... and fought' suggest about the conduct of the campaign?
answers: That the fighting followed long negotiations
That Joshua moved quickly from city to city in a swift campaign of consecutive battles
That there were long pauses between attacks
questions.explanation: The terse wording implies rapid movement and consecutive engagements — a swift campaign.

questions.question: What does 'devoted to destruction' (the ban) reflect about the policy in these conquests?
answers: That cities were usually annexed and their inhabitants integrated
That certain cities were completely destroyed as a religious/military policy
That they only took valuables and left people alive
questions.explanation: The ban (herem) denotes total destruction or dedication to destruction, not integration or mere plunder.

easy.question: Who went from Libnah to Lachish?
answers: Joshua and all Israel with him
Only Joshua alone
Horram king of Gezer
easy.explanation: Verse 31 states Joshua and all Israel went from Libnah to Lachish.

easy.question: What did they do when they reached Lachish?
answers: They turned back to Libnah
They encamped against it and fought it
They signed a peace treaty
easy.explanation: They camped against Lachish and fought against it.

easy.question: When was Lachish taken?
answers: On the first day
On the second day
On the third day
easy.explanation: Verse 32 says Lachish was taken on the second day.

medium.question: What happened to all the souls in Lachish according to the verse?
answers: They were spared and freed
They were struck by the sword and slaughtered
They were taken as allies
medium.explanation: The verse says they struck it with the edge of the sword and all the souls therein were killed.

medium.question: What does the expression 'left none remaining' mean with regard to the inhabitants?
answers: A remnant was kept alive
No people were left alive; total destruction
Some leaders were reserved for rule
medium.explanation: 'Left none remaining' means there were no survivors — total annihilation of the inhabitants.

medium.question: Why did Horam king of Gezer come up according to the verse?
answers: To demand taxes
To help Lachish
To flee from the battle
medium.explanation: The verse explicitly says Horam came up to help Lachish.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'according to all that he had done to Libnah' suggest about Joshua's conduct toward cities?
answers: That Joshua treated each city differently depending on negotiation
That Joshua followed the same pattern of destruction and ban as he did at Libnah
That Libnah aided Lachish earlier
challenge.explanation: The phrase indicates the same measures were taken at Lachish as at Libnah — a consistent policy of destruction.

challenge.question: What does 'left none remaining' imply about the fate of Horam and his people?
answers: Many survivors remained
They were destroyed and no remnant remained
They were taken into Israel’s service
challenge.explanation: The expression indicates they were smitten until none remained — destruction without survivors.

challenge.question: What does Horam's coming to help Lachish indicate about Canaanite city relations?
answers: Cities never helped one another
Cities did assist one another in war — alliances or mutual defense existed among city‑states
